name: The Baluster That Is A Pencil
symptom: A porch balustrade whose balusters are 1 1/4 or 1 1/2 in square in plain stock, or 1 1/4 in turned with almost no belly, or 1/2 in steel rod. They are the same section top to bottom, cast no meaningful shadow, and from thirty feet the rail reads as a horizontal band with a faint grey texture rather than as a course of members. The turned version is worse than the square one: a 1 1/4 in blank cannot be turned to a profile with real relief, because the deepest cove would leave 5/8 in of material, so the turning is reduced to a few shallow rings.

cause.explanation: Balusters are sold by the piece and priced by the blank. A 1 1/4 in square is the standard deck-baluster stock and is what every big-box and every deck supplier carries; a 2 1/2 or 3 in turned baluster is a millwork item on a lead time. Where the rail is a code guard rather than an architectural element — which is how it is scoped on almost every job — nobody specifies the section at all, and the installer takes what the yard sells. The 1 1/4 in square also happens to be the section for which the maximum 4 in sphere spacing works out to the fewest pieces, so it compounds with the spacing fault.
cause.cost_saved: A 1 1/4 in square treated baluster runs 2-4 USD; a 2 1/2 in turned baluster in a durable species or PVC runs 9-22 USD. On a 40 ft porch with 90 balusters, 600-1,600 USD.

rule_violated.statement: A balustrade is 30 to 33 in high with turned or square balusters at 4 to 6 in centres. At 4 in centres the baluster must be substantial or the course cannot read.

rule_violated.ref: vignola-tuscan / pedestal die and cap — the balustrade as the pedestal course
rule_violated.statement: The baluster is a miniature of the column: base, belly, neck and cap, diminishing upward or downward according to the tradition. A member with no belly is not a baluster, it is a picket.

rule_violated.ref: a repeating small member registers by its shadow, not by its outline
rule_violated.statement: A 1 1/4 in square in raking light casts a shadow about 1 1/4 in wide on the deck and nothing on itself, because its faces are flat and its arris is sharp. A 2 1/2 in turned baluster casts a shadow on ITSELF along the belly, which is what gives a balustrade its characteristic soft dark-light-dark banding at distance. The turning is a shadow-generating device.

correct_practice: A residential porch baluster is 2 to 3 in at its widest and not less than 1 3/4 in at its narrowest, whether turned or square. The turned baluster is a small column: a square block at the bottom (the plinth), a swelling belly in the lower third, a neck, and a square block at the top under the rail, with the whole composition proportioned so the belly is at about a third of the height — the same rule as the column's entasis, and for the same reason. Square balusters may be plainer but must keep the section: 2 in square is the working minimum for a period reading and Craftsman work runs 2 1/2 to 3. Where the balustrade is a roof-deck or forecourt balustrade rather than a porch rail, the balusters are larger still — 4 to 6 in at the belly in stone or cast work — because they are read against the sky at a distance. The one dimension that must never be reduced is the belly: it is where the shadow comes from.

fixes.right: Turned or square balusters of 2 to 3 in at their widest, in a durable species or a solid cellular PVC, at 4 to 5 in centres.
fixes.cheap: Square, and thicker. A plain 2x2 (1 1/2 in) is the deck default; a plain 2 in square in the same material costs about 1.50 USD more per piece and reads correctly on Greek Revival, Craftsman, farmhouse vernacular and most Colonial Revival porches, none of which need a turning. Choosing SQUARE AND THICK over TURNED AND THIN is the right trade at every price point below about 12 USD a baluster, because a thin turning is a distorted object and a thick square is simply a plainer one. Second free move: chamfer the arrises of a square baluster, which softens the flat face enough to generate a highlight and costs one router pass.
fixes.dishonest: A thin turned baluster on the assumption that turning compensates for section. It does the opposite: the turning removes material from the already-inadequate section, so the neck of a 1 1/4 in turned baluster is about 5/8 in and the member looks fragile as well as thin. Also dishonest: black-painted balusters to make the rail 'read stronger', which converts the balustrade into a graphic band and is the same evasion as painting a flat muntin.

detection: Measure baluster width against the deck board it stands on — a deck board face is 5 1/2 in — or against the rail cap. A baluster narrower than a quarter of a deck board's face is 1 1/4 in stock. Second check, which needs no reference: look at the SHADOW. In any raking light, a correctly sectioned turned baluster shows a bright highlight down its belly and a dark side, so the balustrade reads as alternating light and dark verticals; a thin baluster shows one flat tone. In a photograph, sample the tonal range across a single baluster: a real one contains both a highlight and a near-black, a thin flat one contains one mid-tone. Third check on turned balusters: measure the widest point against the narrowest. A period turning gives 1.6 to 2.2; a thin one gives 1.15 to 1.3 because there is no material to remove.

test.note: Two inches at the widest point is the working minimum for a porch balustrade to read as a course rather than as a picket fence. Roof-deck and forecourt balustrades take 4 in or more. A useful secondary ratio for turned balusters is max_width / min_width, which should be 1.6 to 2.2 — below 1.4 there was not enough material in the blank to turn a profile.

severity_by_style.why: The turned baluster is the idiom and a thin one is a bad copy of it. Note that Folk Victorian balusters ARE slender by design — see the exception — but slender means 1 3/4 to 2 1/4 in with a real belly, not 1 1/4 in with rings.
The roof balustrade is a silhouette element and needs section to exist against the sky.
The Craftsman baluster is deliberately heavy — 2 1/2 to 3 in square — and thinness contradicts the idiom directly.
The kit's ordinary answer is no rail at all on a three- or four-riser stoop.
Slender gallery balusters are correct there.

exceptions.why: Catalogue spindlework is thin by design and its thinness is the point: the whole porch is a light lattice of slender turned members, and a heavy baluster under a 4 in turned post would invert the assembly.
exceptions.bounds: Slender means 1 3/4 to 2 1/4 in at the belly with a real turned profile — a genuine swelling, a neck and square blocks. It does not mean 1 1/4 in stock with three rings on it. The test is the belly-to-neck ratio, which must still exceed about 1.5, not the absolute width.

exceptions.why: Same: the spindled idiom is built out of the thinnest members the lathe could produce, and that thinness is what distinguishes it from the Free Classic subtype.
exceptions.bounds: As above. The whole assembly must be light and turned: thin posts, thin balusters, spindle frieze.

exceptions.why: Gallery balusters of 1 1/2 to 2 in match the slender colonnettes above them, and the gallery is meant to read as a light screen.
exceptions.bounds: The colonnettes must themselves be slender. A thin baluster under a stout column is the fault.

exceptions.why: Regency ironwork balustrades use members of 1/2 to 3/4 in in wrought or cast iron, and their delicacy is exactly the point — iron's strength permits a section wood cannot.
exceptions.bounds: The member must genuinely be iron, and the pattern must be an iron pattern — scrolls, anthemia, lyres — not a wood profile executed in metal. Steel rod balusters in a wood rail are not Regency ironwork.

confused_with.difference: Section versus interval. The solid-to-void test in that fault catches both together and is the better single measurement; this entry exists because the fix is different — spacing is free to correct at layout, section costs money.

Different member, same mechanism: a member with the right outline and insufficient section, which reads at four feet and dissolves at forty. The balustrade version is more forgiving because the members are closer together.
